name: Netherlands
tagline: Hundreds of English-taught degrees, and the number is shrinking
ownCitizens: If you hold Dutch citizenship, you do not register a right of residence or prove your fee status, and the Netherlands' own student grants and loans are open to you on their ordinary terms; check them, because some depend on where you have lived. Your IB is still a foreign qualification here, so the IB entry rules still apply to you.
summary: The Netherlands is a common choice for IB students in Denmark: hundreds of bachelor's degrees taught entirely in English, three-year programmes, a statutory tuition fee of 2,694 euro for EU students in 2026/27, and a teaching style built on seminars, group work and reading you are expected to do without being chased. Two things have changed. Parliament is working on a law that pushes bachelor's teaching back towards Dutch, and universities have already started cutting or capping English tracks. And the room shortage is genuinely severe - the national student housing monitor published in 2025 estimated a shortage of about 21,500 student rooms in the 19 largest student cities.
whyConsider: Statutory tuition of 2,694 euro for the 2026/27 year applies to you as an EU citizen, at every publicly funded university and hogeschool.
Hundreds of fully English-taught bachelor's degrees, across 13 research universities and a large network of universities of applied sciences.
Research-university bachelor's take three years, like Denmark's; universities of applied sciences take four.
One central portal, Studielink, handles every application to every public institution.
As an EU citizen you can work unlimited hours alongside your studies - no permit, no hour cap.
Hundreds of English-taught bachelor’s degrees, at both research universities and universities of applied sciences.
A full IB Diploma is compared by Nuffic to a VWO diploma, which is the qualification that opens a research university bachelor.
One portal, two deadlines, and a genuinely national process rather than institution-by-institution applications.
The statutory tuition fee is low by international standards and the same at every publicly funded institution.
watchOuts: The Internationalisation in Balance bill (Wet internationalisering in balans, bill 36555) would require bachelor's programmes to be taught mainly in Dutch and force universities to justify every foreign-language programme. On 24 September 2026 it was still before the Tweede Kamer and had not been voted on, but universities are already converting or capping English tracks. Check that the exact programme you want will still run in English in September 2027.

Housing. The national monitor published in 2025 put the shortage at about 21,500 rooms in the 19 largest student cities. Nuffic itself warns of a severe shortage and tells students to start before they arrive. Some universities will not guarantee you a room at all.

Numerus fixus. Popular programmes (medicine, psychology, international business, communication and more) cap places and select. The deadline is 15 January - three and a half months before the normal one, and long before you have IB results.
Numerus fixus programmes can also cap the English-language track separately from the Dutch one, which means the English places can be scarcer than the headline number suggests.

The internationalisation law is the thing to watch. Check in autumn 2026 that the specific programme you want will still be taught in English in September 2027 — not that the university still offers English-taught programmes, but that yours does.

Numerus fixus is not a formality. You may apply to at most two selective programmes in a year, and medicine, dentistry, dental hygiene and physiotherapy allow only one application per programme, so you cannot apply for medicine at two universities. That is a real constraint on strategy and it is decided in January.

"15 January or 1 May" is not the whole story, and believing it will cost you a place. Among these sixteen programmes, the Dutch numerus fixus ones close on 15 January; University College Maastricht closes on 1 April for an EU applicant and 1 February for everyone else; Breda's selective programmes close in Studielink on 1 May but want a portfolio from the previous November; Erasmus wants its own form by 31 January, a fortnight after Studielink; and Twente closed a day early, on 30 April. Read the programme page, not the country page, for the date that binds you.

Studielink does not require a DigiD if you live outside the Netherlands: you create an account by uploading a scan or photo of your passport or EU identity card, which is verified automatically. Do it well before 15 January.
Housing in the university cities is severe. Several institutions warn applicants not to arrive without a confirmed room.
There is no national IB-to-Dutch grade conversion. If you are coming from the Danish system, do not go looking for one.

Several Dutch selections score the grades of your penultimate school year — your DP1 results — and say outright that predicted grades are not used. Rotterdam School of Management and Maastricht both do this. If you are reading this in DP1, those are the grades that will decide it.

ibRecognition.minimumPoints: 24 points and the award of the full IB Diploma is the floor used across Dutch higher education; individual programmes and numerus fixus selection routinely demand far more. Nuffic does not publish a national minimum score.
ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: Nuffic compares the full IB Diploma to a Dutch VWO diploma, which is the qualification that gives access to a research university (universiteit) bachelor's. Programmes that require specific school subjects - maths and physics for engineering, maths for economics and econometrics - normally want those subjects at Higher Level, and each university publishes its own HL/SL list. Check the programme page, not a general page.
ibRecognition.gradeConversion: There is no national IB-to-Dutch points table. Dutch programmes are either open access (you meet the diploma and subject requirements and you are in) or numerus fixus (the university runs its own selection and sets its own weighting of your grades). Ask the individual programme how it scores IB grades.
notes: IB Course Results / certificates without the full Diploma are not equivalent to VWO and do not give access to a research university bachelor's.
A hogeschool (university of applied sciences) bachelor's needs at least a HAVO-equivalent diploma, so a full IB Diploma comfortably clears that bar and takes four years rather than three.

Because your results arrive on 6 July 2027, you will apply and be admitted conditionally and then send your final IB transcript. Confirm the conditional-offer route with each university - the Dutch system is built around Dutch results arriving in June.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: Extensive by European standards, but contracting. Study in NL lists the current English-taught offer across all publicly funded institutions; the number of English-taught bachelor's is falling as universities respond to the internationalisation bill, so any count published today may not hold for 2027 entry.
language.englishProof: Universities set their own English requirements. IB English A or English B at Higher Level is commonly accepted as proof, and many programmes waive a test for anyone who completed a fully English-taught secondary education such as the IB Diploma - but this is decided per programme, not nationally. Otherwise the usual bars are IELTS 6.0-6.5 or TOEFL iBT 80-90. Confirm on the programme page before you rely on a waiver.
notes: You will not need Dutch to study or to live in a student city, but you will need it for many part-time jobs outside hospitality and for most internships in Dutch organisations.

The internationalisation bill's core idea is that bachelor's teaching should be predominantly Dutch, with foreign-language programmes allowed only where they can be justified. That is a direct risk to the English-taught offer you are choosing from.

feeContext.summary: The statutory fee (wettelijk collegegeld), the same at every publicly funded institution. €2,694 for 2026–27; the 2027–28 figure is set annually by government and is not yet published.

sources.title: The statutory tuition fee for 2026–2027 is €2,694. The 2027–2028 figure is not yet published.

feeContext.summary: The institutional fee, set by each institution and substantially higher than the statutory rate. Not established here for 2027–28; check the institution directly.

sectorLandscape.summary: The Netherlands divides higher education in two, and the division matters more than almost anything else a student will read about the country. Research universities (universiteit, WO) and universities of applied sciences (hogeschool, HBO) are parallel systems with different entry qualifications, different lengths, and different purposes — not a ranking. An IB Diploma opens both. Most English-language advice describes only the first.

routes.what: The WO route. A three-year bachelor followed by a one- or two-year master, academic in emphasis and taught by researchers. This is what an IB Diploma is compared to in Dutch terms, and what nearly all English-language guidance is describing.

The HBO route. Four years rather than three, including a substantial placement and often a second one, and built around doing the work rather than studying the discipline. Strong in engineering, business, hotel and event management, design, health and teaching. An IB Diploma is more than sufficient for entry, and Dutch students reach it from HAVO — one level below the VWO an IB compares to.
routes.note: Habitually described as the lesser option, which misreads it. It is the more vocational option, and for a student who wants to be employable in the subject rather than continue to a master, it is frequently the better one.

routes.what: Small selective honours colleges attached to research universities — Amsterdam, Utrecht, Leiden, Maastricht and others. Broad liberal-arts first year narrowing later, taught in English, usually residential, and closer to a US liberal-arts college than anything else in Europe. They select on more than grades and they charge more than the statutory fee.
routes.note: Often a strong fit for an IB student, precisely because the breadth-then-depth structure resembles the Diploma.

routes.what: Art, design, music, dance and theatre, admitting on portfolio or audition. Grades are secondary and the entry process runs on a different calendar and different terms from everything else here.
routes.note: Not covered in detail on this site; these schools do not appear in the ordinary programme listings.

THE NETHERLANDS NEEDS NO RECOGNITION SCHEME, and data/recognition/nl.json is deliberately absent. This was the question ADR 0002 left open and it is now answered from sixteen Opportunities at five institutions rather than predicted. Nearly every Dutch entry requirement found in this pass is published in the IB's own vocabulary — named IB subjects at named IB levels, often with named IB grades. TU Delft: "Mathematics: AA HL + Physics HL". Maastricht: "International Business — Mathematics Analysis and Approaches SL/HL or Mathematics Applications and Interpretation SL/HL". Erasmus School of Economics: "English A HL (4) or English A SL (5) or English B HL (5)". There is nothing to translate and no local subject scale for these requirements to sit on. Nuffic, the recognition body, compares the IB Diploma to a VWO diploma at the level of the whole qualification and publishes no subject or grade conversion at all; ev-nuffic-ib-grades records that absence and why it is a finding rather than a gap.

The one real counter-example is recorded rather than smoothed away. University of Twente's Technical Computer Science asks for "mathematics comparable to a pre-university level, such as VWO Wiskunde B" and names no IB course or level. That is a requirement on a local scale — and it still does not make a case for a Recognition Scheme, because a scheme needs a published equivalence and nobody publishes one: not Twente, not Nuffic. A scheme here could only be invented, and the invention would sit between the university's sentence and the student's transcript, which is the thing ADR 0002 exists to prevent. So the requirement is recorded as kind 'other' with Twente's wording kept whole, and the engine tells the student it cannot check it and sends them to the official page. That Opportunity is the one of the sixteen that assesses as Needs review, and it should be.

The VWO comparison is used here only at qualification level — to establish that a full IB Diploma is required for a research university and that DP Course Results are not enough. It is never used to translate a subject or a grade, because no table exists that would allow it.

A finding worth its own line, because it is the one that would have been destroyed by a convenience: the two IB mathematics courses must be recorded separately and by name. TU Delft accepts only Analysis and Approaches HL and refuses Applications and Interpretation outright. Maastricht accepts Applications and Interpretation at SL for International Business, demands it at HL for Business Analytics and Econometrics, and refuses it entirely for Data Science and Computer Science — one university, one table, three answers. A 'mathematics' family shorthand would have told an Applications and Interpretation student they qualified for all of them.

MODEL FRICTION, all of it in src/ and none of it worked around in the data. (1) src/lib/canonical.mjs denormalise() understands only kind 'local-equivalency', so a requirement written in IB terms projects to entryRequirements: null and a Dutch programme page renders the heading 'And one of these combinations' above an empty list. ADR 0002 added the ib-subject path to the schema and to the engine; this projection into the page templates was not updated with it. (2) The same projection builds extraRequirements from the requirement kinds essay/test/portfolio/interview/audition/other without consulting `mandatory`, so a Selection Factor renders on the programme page under 'On top of the subjects' as though it were an entry requirement. On the Erasmus IBA page a student sees 'Your grade average — 75 per cent of the selection score' in the same list as things they must hold. The answer to 'can a student tell a Requirement from a Selection Factor on the page' is currently no. (3) assess() returns selection.factors and nothing renders it; admission.capacityNote is not rendered anywhere, so numerus fixus capacity and the hard 15 January date reach a page only through an Application Route milestone. (4) The restricted-admission note on a programme page is Danish copy — it talks about quota cut-offs and national intake policy — and it now appears on Dutch pages. (5) src/pages/programmes.mjs describes the planner as checking 'every English-taught programme in Denmark' and converting subjects 'using the Danish Agency's official table'; it now also checks sixteen Dutch ones and converts nothing for them.

MODEL FRICTION in the schema, found mechanically by the validator. A Requirement's `kind` enum and admission.selection[].type are two different vocabularies and neither contains the other. 'gpa', 'subject-grades', 'lottery' and 'work-experience' are selection types and are not requirement kinds — which means the four commonest Dutch ranking criteria cannot be named on the Requirement that carries them. They are recorded as kind 'other' or 'activity' with the precise mechanism in admission.selection and a note on each saying why.

MODEL FRICTION with no clean answer: a step that is compulsory and unweighted. The Dutch matching procedure (studiekeuzecheck) is exactly this, and so are TU Delft's Matching phase, Erasmus School of Economics' pass/fail curriculum activity and Twente's mandatory questionnaire and matching event. mandatory: true makes the engine answer 'needs review' for every student on a question that is not about eligibility; mandatory: false says it ranks them, which the sources explicitly deny — TU Delft: "they do not influence your place in the ranking". Recorded in admission.selection with weight 'none' plus a meta note, which is the least wrong shape available.

A near-miss between Requirement and Selection Factor that the model handles well and is worth keeping as the worked example: Rotterdam School of Management awards selection points only from 33 IB points upwards. Below 33 an applicant is still eligible and their application still stands; they simply score nothing and are therefore not in the running. Recorded as a Selection Factor with minPoints 33. Recorded as a Requirement it would tell a 32-point student they cannot apply, which is false.

A build check in src/lib/data.mjs treats every canonical institution as Danish and compares its id against the image keys derived from countries/nl.json. Canonical ids nl-um, nl-eur and nl-buas collided with the country profile's own entries for the same three universities and failed the build with 'one of them would show the other's photograph' — a false positive, since they are the same institutions. Since data/countries/nl.json was out of scope, the canonical ids were renamed to nl-maastricht, nl-erasmus and nl-breda-uas instead. The check is still wrong and will catch the next Destination that migrates.

What works end to end, checked rather than assumed: all sixteen Dutch Opportunities are assessed in /planner/ against a Danish IB profile — thirteen meet, Nanobiology is Possible with action for want of Biology HL, Technical Computer Science is Needs review for the reason above. The engine's sentence reads 'Your Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches HL meets HL. This requirement is published in IB terms, so nothing is converted.' That is ADR 0002 working as designed on a Destination with no Recognition Scheme, which is the test the ADR said had to pass.

Coverage as at 2026-09-23: 5 institutions, 16 Programmes, 16 Opportunities. Research universities TU Delft, Erasmus Rotterdam, Maastricht and Twente (universiteit); Breda University of Applied Sciences (hogeschool); University College Maastricht covers the university college route. The kunstacademie / conservatorium route is still unresearched and is recorded as such in sectorLandscape.

Not established across the pass: how any Dutch institution handles a conditional offer pending IB results published on about 6 July, except at Maastricht, where the certified diploma is an enrolment task due 31 August rather than an admission task. Capacity figures for TU Delft Nanobiology, all four Breda programmes and Maastricht International Business. Whether Breda's selection runs under the numerus fixus article of the WHW at all, which is why its 1 May deadline differs from the national 15 January.

deadlines.label: Studielink opens for the 2027-2028 academic year
deadlines.notes: Published with its year by the University of Amsterdam: "You can submit your enrolment application for the academic year 2027-2028 in Studielink from 1 October 2026 till 15 January 2027." Studielink's information site info.studielink.nl states the 15 January and 1 May deadlines without saying when applications open, so the opening date is taken from the university's page.

deadlines.label: Numerus fixus (selective) programmes
deadlines.notes: Absolute, and published to the minute: Studielink's own guidance is "until 23:59 on 15 January", and the University of Amsterdam states the 2027 date: "from 1 October 2026 till 15 January 2027". You may apply to at most two numerus fixus programmes in one academic year. Medicine, Dentistry, Dental Hygiene and Physiotherapy allow only one application per programme, so you cannot apply for Medicine at two universities. Selection then runs between 15 January and 15 April; what happens on 15 April, and what you then have to do, are entries of their own.

deadlines.label: Numerus fixus ranking numbers issued
deadlines.notes: Published as "Applicants in the selection procedure will receive a ranking number via Studielink on 15 April". Nothing is required of you on the day itself — but this is the day the two-week clock starts for anyone offered a place, so it is the day to start watching Studielink rather than the day to relax. A ranking number above the number of places is not a refusal: places freed by students who do not accept are offered down the list, so ranking 101 of 100 places can still become an offer.

deadlines.label: Accept your numerus fixus place in Studielink
deadlines.notes: The deadline is two weeks from your own offer, not a day in the calendar. Published as "If you are offered a place, you have to accept this place via Studielink within two weeks", and Studielink is explicit that a place not accepted in time "will be assigned to another student automatically". If your offer arrives with the ranking numbers on 15 April, that puts you at the end of April; if it arrives later, because someone above you declined, your fortnight starts then. This is the most expensive thing on the Dutch page to miss and the only one with no date you can set in advance, so the practical answer is to check Studielink from 15 April onwards rather than to wait for an email.

deadlines.label: All other (non-selective) bachelor's programmes
deadlines.year: 2027 entry - Nuffic states the deadline as 1 May; individual universities may set an earlier one
deadlines.notes: Studielink closes at 23:59 on 1 May. The government’s rule is what makes it an equal-consideration date: apply by 1 May and you are entitled to admission to a programme you qualify for ("Aanmelding tot en met 1 mei betekent ook recht op toelating"); a first application after 1 May "kan door de opleiding geweigerd worden" - the programme may still take you, but it does not have to. Some programmes close earlier for capacity or matching reasons, and the programme’s own date is the one that binds.

steps: From autumn 2026, use the Study in NL programme finder to check whether each programme you want is still taught in English for 2027 entry and whether it has a numerus fixus.

Create a Studielink account. With a Dutch address you log in with DigiD; without one you create an account by uploading a scan or photo of your passport or EU identity card, which Studielink verifies automatically. Then add your programme choices.
Apply by 15 January 2027 for any numerus fixus programme, and by 1 May 2027 for open-access programmes.
Complete the university's own application in its student portal: motivation letter, CV, predicted IB grades, transcript, proof of English, sometimes a test or interview.
For open-access programmes, take part in the matching or study check activity - at many universities this is compulsory even though the advice is non-binding.
Numerus fixus results land on 15 April; accept your place within two weeks or it goes to the next person on the list.

Send your final IB transcript as soon as results are released on 6 July 2027 — and ask your IB coordinator to put each university on your transcript list before 5 July, because from that date you request transcripts yourself through rrs.ibo.org at $19 each instead of free through the school. Then enrol, pay the tuition fee, and register with the municipality once you have an address.
application.selectionNotes: Two worlds. Open access: meet the diploma, subject and English requirements and you are admitted, with no competition on grades. Numerus fixus: the programme sets a number of places and runs decentrale selectie, scoring you on grades, motivation, tests, interviews or a written assignment - each programme designs its own procedure and publishes it. Medicine is numerus fixus everywhere and is the hardest route in the country.

tuitionEuEea.value: 2,694 EUR per year (statutory tuition fee, wettelijk collegegeld)

tuitionNonEu.value: Institutional fee set by each university; Nuffic gives a range of roughly 9,000-20,000 EUR per year for a bachelor's

costs.applicationFee: None for EU/EEA applicants via Studielink. Nuffic notes that some institutions charge non-EEA applicants an application or handling fee of about 75-100 EUR.

livingCostMonthly.value: 1,000-1,500 EUR per month. Nuffic's breakdown (Nibud data, 2024): rent 561, groceries 244, leisure and sport 239, Dutch basic health insurance 133 if you work, transport 67, books and materials 41. Rent alone ranges from about 450 to 1,000 depending on the city.

notes: The statutory fee is set by the government each year and has risen steadily, so budget for a higher figure in 2027/28 than the 2026/27 amount.

You pay the statutory fee only if you hold EU/EEA, Swiss or Surinamese nationality (or a qualifying Dutch residence permit) and do not already hold a degree at that level from a Dutch government-funded institution.

funding.note: The programme must be SU-approved, and outside the Nordics SU is capped at four years (48 klip). Apply to Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen before you leave.

funding: Dutch student finance (studiefinanciering) from DUO: open to EU/EEA nationals only in specific cases. Nuffic states plainly that EU students may qualify 'in specific cases' without listing them, and DUO assesses each applicant. Check your own eligibility with DUO directly before counting on it.
Tuition fee loan (collegegeldkrediet) from DUO, for students who are entitled to Dutch student finance.

Institutional scholarships: most universities run a small number of merit scholarships for first-year internationals. They are competitive and rarely cover more than tuition. Search them through the Study in NL Studyfinder.
Part-time work. As an EU citizen you can work without a permit or hour limit, and student jobs in hospitality, supermarkets and university departments are widely available in student cities.
workRights: EU, EEA and Swiss students can work alongside their studies without restrictions - no work permit and no maximum hours (Study in NL / Nuffic, https://www.studyinnl.org/finances/scholarship-and-funding-for-eu-students). Non-EU students need their employer to hold a work permit and are limited to seasonal summer work or a small number of hours per week; check the IND rules before accepting a job.
residency: As an EU citizen you do not need a visa or residence permit. What you do need is a Dutch address and a BSN (citizen service number): register with the gemeente (municipality) of the town you live in shortly after arrival, bringing your passport, your birth certificate and proof of your address. Without a BSN you cannot open most bank accounts, take out insurance or be paid legally. Registration requires a registered address, which is one more reason the housing problem is not just about comfort.
housing: This is the hardest part of studying in the Netherlands and you should plan around it, not hope. The Landelijke Monitor Studentenhuisvesting 2025 (Kences and the Ministry of Housing) estimated a shortage of about 21,500 student rooms in the 19 largest student cities for 2024-25, only slightly down from 22,800 a year earlier. Nuffic describes a 'severe housing shortage' and says there is not enough student accommodation for everyone. Nuffic budgets rent at about 561 EUR a month (Nibud, 2024), more in Amsterdam and Utrecht, less in Enschede, Groningen, Maastricht and Tilburg. Start the search the moment you apply, not when you are admitted. Ask your university's housing office first - some institutions reserve a block of rooms for first-year internationals and those open on a fixed date, often in spring. Use DUWO, Kamernet, Pararius and the university's own listings. Nuffic warns never to sign a contract for a room you have not seen (ask for a video tour) and never to pay brokerage fees, which are not required by law.
healthcare: Bring your blue European Health Insurance Card from the country where you are insured. If you only study, the EHIC plus that coverage is normally enough. The moment you take a paid job or a paid internship in the Netherlands, Dutch law requires you to take out Dutch basic health insurance (basisverzekering) - Nuffic budgets about 133 EUR a month for it. If you are on Dutch basic insurance and on a low income you can usually claim zorgtoeslag (healthcare allowance) from the tax office, which refunds part of the premium. Register with a local GP (huisarts) early; in student cities the good practices fill up.

sources.title: BUas's four selective bachelor programmes are Hotel Management, Creative Media & Game Technologies, Creative Business and Applied Data Science & Artificial Intelligence. The Studielink deadline for a BUas programme with selection is 1 May, and each programme selects on portfolio, assignment, test and interview rather than on grades.
sources.quote: The official deadline to make an enrolment application in Studielink for bachelor programmes with selection is 1 May. [...] Hotel Management — Besides the formal admission requirements, there are several selection criteria. First and foremost, we are looking for intrinsically motivated individuals. [...] students with a diploma from a non-Dutch educational institution: A personal video message. [...] Creative Media & Game Technologies — Preselection is based on the submission of an assignment and portfolio specific to each discipline, with a pass/fail grading system. [...] Applicants have four submission deadlines for their assignments, each by 23:59 CET: November 27, January 15, March 05, May 15. [...] Creative Business — STAGE A: 50% [application letter, resume, study skills test, previous knowledge test]; Stage B: 50% [interview]. [...] Applied Data Science & Artificial Intelligence — 20% Motivation; 20% Suitability and communication skills; 60% Mathematics test + experience and presentation. Scoring and selection: >70% = Selected; 60-70% = Waiting list; <60% = Not selected.

routes.label: Applying to Maastricht University for autumn 2027

milestones.label: Maastricht applications open in Studielink
milestones.note: Applications for 2027-2028 open on 1 October. University College Maastricht reviews them on a rolling basis from then until its deadline.

sources.title: Studielink opens for applications for the 2027-2028 academic year on Thursday 1 October 2026, and the closing date for a numerus fixus programme is 15 January 2027. It gives 1 May as the deadline for most other programmes, without a year.

University College Maastricht has 250 places, a two-round selective admission of document review then an online interview in English, and deadlines of 1 February 2027 for non-EU/EEA applicants and 1 April 2027 for EU/EEA and Swiss applicants. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis. First-year students must earn 45 of 60 ECTS or be excluded from the programme for six years.
sources.quote: At UCM, we are looking for highly motivated students with a genuine passion for academics. To find the right match between your academic interests and what UCM offers, we use a selective admissions process. Each year, we have 250 places available for new students. [...] 1 February 2027, 23:59 CET — Deadline for applicants with a non-EU/EEA nationality [...] 1 April 2027, 23:59 CET — Deadline for applicants with an EU/EEA or Swiss nationality [...] At UCM, we review applications on a rolling basis, so you can apply at any time up until the deadline. [...] First round: The Board of Admissions will review your application documents and let you know by email if you have been selected for an interview. Second round: If selected, you will be invited for an online interview in English with a UCM academic staff member. The interview takes about 30-45 minutes and focuses on your academic plans and how you see your education at UCM supporting these goals. [...] in your first year of the programme, you must obtain a minimum of 45 out of 60 ECTS credits.

milestones.label: University College Maastricht closes for non-EU/EEA applicants
milestones.note: Studielink application and every admission task in Maastricht's own MyApplication portal, both by this date.

milestones.label: International Business numerus fixus application closes

sources.title: International Business is a numerus fixus programme selected by the university itself. The ranking is one third International Classroom Essay, one third CV and supporting documents, one third the grades of the applicant's penultimate school year. Failing the International Classroom requirement removes an applicant from the ranking entirely.
sources.quote: International Business is a numerus fixus programme with selection by the educational institution. This means that you go through a selection process after applying. Due to the limited number of places we cannot offer a place to every applicant who meets the admission requirements. [...] Deadline for all applicants to: apply via Studielink; complete all admission tasks [...] in the MyApplication portal. [15 January, 23:59 CET] [...] Outcome selection procedure and publication ranking number [15 April, 23:59 CET] [...] Their assessment is based on your: International Classroom Essay (33%); Curriculum vitae + supporting documents (33%); Grades of your penultimate year of secondary school (33%). [...] If your profile is not sufficient to meet the International Classroom requirement, you will not be included in the ranking procedure. This means that you will not be able to start this bachelor's programme. [...] This decision will also be valid for the bachelor's programme in Economics and Business Economics, since the International Classroom requirement is the same for both programmes.

routes.label: Applying to the Netherlands for autumn 2027

milestones.label: Create your Studielink account
milestones.note: Not an official deadline. With a Dutch address you log in with DigiD, which the government says takes about five days. Without one you upload a scan or photo of your passport or EU identity card and Studielink verifies it automatically. Either way, do it well before 15 January.

sources.title: An applicant without DigiD creates a Studielink account by uploading a scan or photo of a passport or European identity card, which is verified automatically by an online tool.

contextNotes.text:
The Netherlands has long drawn IB students with English-taught bachelor programmes, and that provision is now shrinking. A law going through would require bachelor programmes to be taught mainly in Dutch unless the institution justifies otherwise, and institutions have begun converting and capping English tracks ahead of it.

The practical consequence for someone applying in 2027 is narrow and specific: a list of English-taught programmes compiled today is not evidence about September 2027. Check the programme page for the intake you want, in autumn 2026, and take the university’s own current wording over any aggregated list including this one.
contextNotes.attribution: The Internationalisation in Balance bill and institutions’ own announcements
contextNotes.whatThisIsNot: Not a statement that the Netherlands is closing to international students, and not a reason to rule it out. It is a reason to verify one specific programme rather than trust a count.

sources.title: Selection for numerus fixus programmes runs between 15 January and 15 April, ranking numbers are issued on 15 April, and an offer must be accepted within two weeks.

contextNotes.topic: There is no Dutch equivalent of the Danish conversion table
contextNotes.text:
A student arriving from the Danish system will look for the table that turns IB points into a local average, and there is not one. Nuffic describes the IB scale and states that a full Diploma is comparable to a VWO diploma, and stops there.

That is not an omission, it is a different design. Dutch admission to a non-selective programme is an entitlement: hold a qualifying diploma, apply by the deadline, and you are in. Where demand exceeds places, the institution runs its own selection on its own criteria, which may weigh grades alongside a motivation letter, a test or an interview. So the question shifts from "what average do I need" to "is this programme selective, and what does that institution actually select on".
contextNotes.attribution: Nuffic's education-system pages for the IB
contextNotes.whatThisIsNot: Not a claim that grades do not matter. They matter a great deal in numerus fixus selection — they are simply not converted to a national scale first.

sources.title: Nuffic describes the IB grading scale and the diploma requirements but publishes no conversion from IB points to the Dutch 1–10 scale.

contextNotes.topic: Hogeschool is not a lesser universiteit
contextNotes.text:
A common misreading of the Dutch system by people outside it is that hogeschool means "not quite university". It does not. They are parallel systems with different purposes: the universiteit teaches the discipline and leads to a master, the hogeschool teaches the work and leads to a job, with four years including substantial placements.

Dutch students arrive at a hogeschool from HAVO and at a universiteit from VWO, and because an IB Diploma is compared to VWO, an IB student can choose either. That is a genuine choice and it is worth making deliberately rather than by default. A student who wants to be employable in a field rather than continue studying it is often better served by the hogeschool, and will rarely be told so.
contextNotes.attribution: Nuffic's comparison of the IB Diploma to a VWO diploma, read alongside the structure of the two sectors

sources.title: Nuffic compares the full IB Diploma to a Dutch VWO diploma, and DP Course Results to vwo-deelcertificaten for the subjects passed.
sources.quote: Diploma of the International Baccalaureate — a VWO diploma. Bilingual Diploma of the International Baccalaureate — a VWO diploma. DP Course result — VWO modular certificates (vwo-deelcertificaten) for the subjects with a pass. Career-related Programme Certificate — at least a HAVO diploma.

additionalGuidance.title: More about studying here
additionalGuidance.text: The Netherlands is a common choice for an IB student in Denmark who wants an English-taught degree in Europe: hundreds of bachelor programmes taught entirely in English, three-year research-university degrees, a low statutory fee, and an application process that runs through one portal. All of that is still true and the first part of it is contracting, because a law now going through requires bachelor programmes to be taught mainly in Dutch unless the institution can justify otherwise. Universities have already begun converting and capping English tracks.
